entries.claim: A pre-flight refusal is not guaranteed to write nothing: `satisfied` is arbitrary caller code and is executed before the refusal result is returned.
entries.failure_scenario: A caller can supply `{ condition: 'destination is safe', satisfied: () => { writeFileSync(target, ''); return false; } }`. `runTransition` invokes that function at line 151, the function truncates `target`, and then the primitive returns `{ ok:false, refused: ... }`. No transition step ran, but the refused transition has already modified the tree. The API/JSDoc promises that an unsatisfied condition means “no thunk runs, nothing is written,” but neither the implementation nor the `PreflightCondition` contract requires or enforces a side-effect-free predicate; the tests cover only pure predicates.

counter_evidence.note: Downgraded medium -> low: real as a documentation-precision point, not a correctness defect. Neither live call site passes preflight at all - planning.mjs:6023 (cmdRenumber, stop-at-first-failure) and planning.mjs:6495 (cmdMilestonePrune, continue-past-failure) both omit the key, so preflight defaults to [] and the cited loop body at file-transition.mjs:148-152 never runs in production. The scenario therefore requires a caller that does not exist. The same JSDoc block already bounds its own scope at file-transition.mjs:141 - "this classifies a transition, it does not police its caller" - which is exactly the enforcement the finding asks for, and JavaScript cannot enforce a side-effect-free callback in any case. What survives is narrow: the sentence at file-transition.mjs:124 says "no thunk runs, nothing is written" where only the first clause is enforceable, and it should read as a statement about what runTransition does rather than a guarantee over arbitrary caller predicates.
